analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $6.75 and then locks it to half the average private wage.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate labor committee on March 11, 1993 and never received a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour in four yearly steps to $6.75 by September 1996, restoring much of the buying power the minimum wage had lost since 1978. After that, it would have adjusted the wage automatically every year to half of what average private nonfarm workers earn, so Congress would no longer have to act to keep it from eroding. It was introduced by Senator Paul Wellstone, never gained a cosponsor, and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, roughly at or below the wage floor for hourly jobs in retail, food service, and other low-paying work, would see their pay rise in four steps to $6.75 an hour, with automatic increases afterward. The bill's own findings note the increase would reach low-wage workers concentrated in inner-city communities and lift the minimum wage toward its 1978 value.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage in four steps from $4.25 to $4.85 (September 1993), $5.55 (1994), $6.20 (1995), and $6.75 (1996), which the bill's findings say would restore the wage to roughly its 1978 purchasing power.

Beginning September 1997, automatically adjusts the wage each June to 50 percent of average hourly earnings for nonfarm, nonsupervisory private workers, as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, with no reductions allowed year to year.

The bill's findings state the minimum wage had fallen from 47 percent of the average private wage in 1978 to about 40 percent in 1992, and that indexing would replace large, belated congressional adjustments with modest annual increases.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers, especially labor-intensive businesses like restaurants, retail, and other service employers, would bear the higher wage bill in four annual steps. Consumers could see some of that passed through in prices; small businesses with many entry-level workers would face the sharpest cost increases.

drawbacks.text: The four-step increase from $4.25 to $6.75 would raise wage costs by nearly 60 percent over three years for employers who pay the minimum, a faster climb than the smaller, slower increases Congress ultimately debated in that era, and small businesses with thin margins would feel it first.

Tying the wage to half of average private earnings means automatic annual increases with no congressional review, which supporters called protection against erosion and critics could view as removing elected officials' ability to weigh economic conditions before each increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a substantial, lasting pay increase to the country's lowest-paid workers and, through indexing, ended the cycle in which the minimum wage loses value for years between congressional adjustments. The real cost falls on employers of low-wage labor, and the automatic formula removes flexibility in a downturn. The core trade is straightforward: money in low-wage workers' paychecks versus higher labor costs for the businesses that employ them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, where it sat without a markup or floor vote until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the bill in the Senate on March 11, 1993, with introductory remarks on the floor the same day.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on March 11, 1993, and no further action is recorded in the bill's history.
Under the bill's own findings, the minimum wage stood at $4.25 an hour following the 1990-1991 increases, and the bill died with the Congress without that level being raised through this legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers were better off because the bill never advanced, since it would have raised their wage costs in steps to $6.75 an hour. Low-wage workers gained nothing from the bill itself; the federal minimum remained at $4.25, the level the bill's text says was in effect, meaning their buying power continued to erode as the bill's findings described.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks, and referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 11, 1993 and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the 103rd Congress, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so there is no record of where parties stood beyond the Democratic sponsor himself.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These employers pay a large share of minimum-wage workers and would have borne the four-step increase to $6.75 an hour. The wage floor these businesses profit from keeping low is the paycheck the bill would have raised.
A near-60 percent wage increase over three years would have been a real cost for small employers, though their lowest-paid employees are the same workers the bill aimed to help.
